title: Future-Proofing Your Career
hook: You won't be replaced by AI so much as by a person who uses it well. The hedge isn't out-typing the machine — it's getting fluent with it while doubling down on what's stubbornly human.
key_points: Become the person who uses AI well in your field — that's the near-term edge.
Lean into human strengths: judgment, relationships, creativity, hands-on skill, accountability.
Treat learning AI tools as a normal, ongoing job skill, like email or spreadsheets.
Stay adaptable — specific tools change fast; the habit of learning them is what lasts.
content_html: "Will AI take my job?" naturally leads to a more useful question: "What do I actually do about it?" The most repeated piece of career advice in the AI era has become a cliché because it's largely true — in the near term, you're far more likely to be out-competed by a person using AI well than by AI on its own. That reframes the goal. The hedge isn't to hide from the technology or to try to beat it at the things it's fast at; it's to become the person in your field who's genuinely good at using it, so the boring parts of your work compress and your output and range expand.
extra_html: The complementary move is to lean into what AI is bad at, because that's where durable human value concentrates. AI predicts plausible text; it doesn't truly understand, can't take responsibility, has no real relationships, and has no stake in the outcome. So the skills that hold their value are the human ones: judgment (knowing which answer is actually right and what matters), relationships and trust (the reason people want to work with you), creativity with a point of view, hands-on physical skill, and accountability for decisions. Practically, treat learning AI tools as a normal, ongoing part of any job — the way email and spreadsheets once became baseline skills — and stay adaptable, because the specific apps will keep changing while the meta-skill of picking them up quickly is what actually protects you. The future of work isn't human or AI; for most jobs it's humans with AI, and the people who internalize that early give themselves the biggest cushion.

related.title: AI & Jobs
related.hook: AI is less likely to take your whole job than to take certain tasks within it. The pattern through history: tools reshape work faster than they erase it.

related.title: AI at Work
related.hook: The biggest everyday payoff from AI is at work: drafting the email, summarizing the meeting, untangling the spreadsheet formula. The trick is using it without leaking secrets or trust.

related.title: Using AI Responsibly
related.hook: The point of AI literacy isn't to use AI for everything — it's to use it well: check its work, be honest that you used it, and know the moments to put it down.

flashcards.prompt: What's the most practical way to future-proof your career against AI?

choices.text: Get fluent using AI in your field while strengthening your human skills
Avoid AI entirely and hope it goes away
Try to do routine tasks faster than the machine

flashcards.explanation_html: Competing on speed with AI is a losing game. The edge is becoming someone who wields it well, paired with judgment, relationships, and creativity it can't replicate.

flashcards.prompt: Which human strengths are hardest for AI to replace?
flashcards.back_html: Judgment, relationships and trust, genuine creativity, hands-on physical skill, and accountability — the things a statistical text-predictor can't own.
